content.title: About
content.content: Pita with fruit is a soft, flat bread that incorporates pieces of dried fruit (raisins, apricots, dates) and sometimes aromatic spices. The dough is made from wheat flour, water, yeast, and a small amount of sugar, after which finely chopped dried fruits are folded in, giving a mildly sweet flavor and fragrant aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pita is a staple in Middle Eastern cuisines, and the addition of dried fruit makes it popular as a sweet snack.
Dried fruits retain most of their vitamins and minerals while concentrating sugars, increasing the nutritional density.
Pita dough typically contains no added fats, making it lighter than many other breads.
Pita can be split and filled with a variety of toppings, from cheese to vegetables; the fruit version is often served as a dessert.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dried fruits are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Raisins and apricots provide B‑vitamins, vitamin K, and small amounts of vitamin C.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Dried fruits supply potassium, magnesium, and iron, important for electrolyte balance and blood formation.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Naturally occurring sugars in the fruit quickly replenish glucose stores, making pita a good source of fast energy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in dried fruit help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Dried fruits contain concentrated sugars, so people with diabetes should limit consumption.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Traditional pita is made from wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in those with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The added fruit increases the calorie count, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit pita can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, split and spread with cottage cheese, honey, or nut butter. It also pairs well with yogurt, ice cream, or as a base for sweet sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pita in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator – up to a week. Before eating, check for any signs of mold or hardened fruit pieces.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat crackers with reduced fat are light, crunchy biscuits made from whole wheat flour, containing less fat than regular crackers. They have a mildly salty flavor and are suitable for diet-conscious eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat crackers often use whole‑grain flour, increasing their fiber content.
Fat reduction is achieved by replacing part of the oil with air‑leavening baking techniques.
They are a popular low‑calorie alternative to bread for snackers.
In many countries they are served alongside soups and salads.
Various flavor versions exist: with seeds, herbs, cheese, etc.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers deliver slow‑release energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium (when unsalted)
items.content: Unsalted versions are appropriate for those monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat crackers contain gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some flavored varieties can be salty; choose low‑sodium options if you have hypertension.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: Check for preservatives or flavor enhancers if you are sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, paired with low‑fat cheese, hummus, vegetable dips, or used as a base for canapés. They are convenient to pack in a bag or lunchbox.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to preserve crispness.

kale-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Kale, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Kale is a leafy cruciferous vegetable known for its high levels of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. This product is frozen, pre‑cooked without added fat, and ready to use in dishes without further cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale is often called a “superfood” because of its dense nutrient profile.
Freezing preserves most of its vitamins, especially vitamin C and carotenoids.
Kale is a close relative of broccoli, Brussels sprouts, and cabbage.
In the wild, kale grows in coastal regions of Europe and Asia, tolerating strong winds.
Its fiber content is higher than that of most leafy greens.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Kale provides over 500 % of the daily value for vitamin K, which is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Kale contains polyphenols and carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Mineral dense
items.content: It supplies calcium, magnesium, and iron, nutrients important for bones, muscles, and blood formation.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein and fiber source
items.content: Kale offers plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and healthy digestion.

items.title: Possible interaction with blood thinners
items.content: The high vitamin K content may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Kale contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen cooked kale can be added to soups, stews, smoothies, salads, or used as a side dish. It reheats quickly in the microwave or a skillet without added oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep kale in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole evaporated milk is milk from which a portion of water has been removed and then sweetened with sugar. It has a thick, creamy consistency, a mildly sweet taste, and a long shelf life. It is commonly used in confectionery, desserts, and beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Evaporated milk was invented in the 19th century as a way to extend the shelf life of dairy products.
During World War II it became a vital food for troops because it did not require refrigeration.
In many countries it is a traditional ingredient for sweet dishes such as "milky pudding" or "flan".
There is an unsweetened version—unsweetened evaporated milk—used in cooking for a neutral flavor.
Evaporated milk is often used as a substitute for fresh milk in recipes that need a thicker texture.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Whole evaporated milk provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: It supplies high‑quality dairy protein that aids tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sugar and fat give a quick source of energy, useful in demanding situations.

items.title: Nutrient fats
items.content: Whole milk includes saturated and monounsaturated fats that can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The product contains a lot of sugar, which can contribute to cavities and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of sugar and fat, it is calorie‑rich and should be consumed in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant may experience digestive discomfort after consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may have allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add evaporated milk to baked goods, cakes, ice cream, coffee, smoothies, and sauces. It can be diluted with hot water to create a sweet milky base or used as a filling for pancakes and waffles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep it refrigerated and use within 2–3 weeks. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

pizza-with-pepperoni-from-school-lunch-t.title: Pizza with Pepperoni (School Lunch, Thick Crust)

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with pepperoni is a popular school‑lunch option. The dough has a thick crust, topped with slices of spicy pepperoni sausage, tomato sauce, and mozzarella cheese. It is baked in an oven, giving the crust a crunchy texture and the cheese a uniform melt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepperoni is an American version of Italian salami, made from pork and beef seasoned with paprika and other spices.
A thick crust requires a longer baking time, resulting in a denser, more filling slice.
Pizza is often included in school menus as a source of protein and carbohydrates needed for children’s growth.
Some schools serve pizza with vegetable sides to balance the meal.
Tomato sauce contains lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pepperoni and cheese provide a substantial amount of protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Mozzarella cheese supplies calcium, important for bone development in children.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: The tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant with heart‑protective properties.

items.title: Energy‑dense
items.content: The thick crust offers lasting satiety thanks to complex carbohydrates.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and meat ingredients contain vitamins B1, B2, and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pepperoni and prepared sauce can be salty, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and processed meat contain saturated fats that should be limited in the diet.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy should avoid this pizza.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The thick crust makes the pizza more calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the pizza hot, cutting it into individual slices. For a more balanced meal, pair it with fresh vegetables or a salad. Optional toppings include fresh basil or oregano for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to keep the crust crisp.
